newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore banks' profit growth to peak in 1996.
newsitem.headline: Singapore banks' profit growth to peak in 1996.

text.p: Singapore's banks are on course for a record year in 1996 but growth rates have probably peaked and 1997 will begin to show signs of the current economic slowdown in Southeast Asia, analysts say.

"This year will be good but we think 1997 will be tougher with the slowdown in industrial output beginning to show up, particularly in the second half," said Mano Sabnani, research director at DBS Securities, the brokerage arm of the Development Bank of Singapore (DBS).

Despite this, analysts say Singapore's big four banks -- DBS, Overseas Union Bank Ltd, Oversea-Chinese Banking Corp and United Overseas Bank Ltd (UOB) -- remain attractive and safe investments due to their strong balance sheets and lucrative regional operations.
Bank profits tend to lag major economic trends by up to 18 months because of the time it takes to decide on and arrange loans and investments.
As a result, Singapore's banks are still reaping the rewards of the city-state's buoyant economy in 1994 and 1995 and the wild property boom which accompanied it.

But after a 10.2 percent jump in gross domestic product (GDP) in 1994 and an 8.8 percent rise in 1995, Singapore's economic growth is expected to slow to close to seven percent this year due to a slump in its key electronics industry.
This slowdown, together with a series of recent government rulings designed to curb property price inflation and stem credit expansion, is squeezing bank borrowings.
Total loan growth in Singapore is expected to fall to 11-12 percent in 1997, from 14-15 percent at the end of 1996 and 19.8 percent in 1995, according to a report by DBS Securities.
This will be reflected in the banks' bottom lines.
"Earnings growth will moderate," said Beatrice Woo, banking analyst at ING-Barings in Singapore. "There are just too many uncertain, and possibly negative, factors in the equation."

Singapore's most profitable bank, UOB, is set to show a 12 percent increase in its 1996 profits to around S$708 million (US$502 million), according to The Estimate Directory (TED) of average analysts' forecasts.
UOB's profit growth rate may rise slightly to 13 percent in 1997, TED says.
But this is the only one of the four likely to show an increased growth rate.

OCBC's profits are expected to jump 17 percent in 1996 to S$707 million but rise only 13 percent in 1997. OUB is set to see a 20 percent rise in 1996 to S$312 million but this will fall to 16 percent in 1997.
DBS is expected to show an unchanged rise in profits in 1997 and 1996 of 13 percent, turning in S$669 million in 1996.
But analysts still say Singapore banks remain attractive.
"It makes sense for regional investors to get into Singapore banks," said Violet Soh, research manager at brokerage Fraser Securities. "They are really true blue banking stocks."
"They are safe, very well capitalised and they are also regionalising. So through them you can also have safe exposure to the Hong Kong, Malaysian and Indonesian markets."
Almost all the Singapore brokerages rate OUB as a buy or accumulate based on what they see as its aggressive expansion into Southeast Asian regional banking.
OCBC is also generally rated either as a buy or accumulate thanks to its income from the property market.
DBS is widely viewed as either an accumulate or hold.
Even UOB, the biggest but slowest growing of the four, is favoured by Soh as inexpensive: "I like all the Singapore banks at the right price," she said.
